_defaultToolsRationale: codemode stays next to read, bash, edit and write, so scripts can run tool calls in parallel and filter large output before the model reads it. A script calls bash through ctx.executeTool(), which fires the same tool_call event as a direct call, so extensions/shell-deny.ts applies the deny rules there too: keep that extension loaded while codemode is on.
_extensionsRationale: The built-in llama.cpp extension is off because no llama.cpp router runs here: the local models come from the nativ provider in models.json, on the port that extension takes for its own default.
_enabledModelsRationale: The Claude entries are the models this account's Claude Max subscription covers. They go directly through the anthropic provider and never through OpenRouter, which bills the same models to credits. Only the newest version of each Claude line stays in the scope: when a successor enters, its predecessor leaves. Before a Claude model enters the scope, send it a one-word prompt with `pi --print --model anthropic/{id}` through the plan login, and drop a model that answers that the plan does not include it. Send the same probe to a model already in the scope as a control. Fable models draw at most 50% of the weekly limits (https://support.claude.com/en/articles/15424964-claude-fable-models-on-your-plan). When every anthropic model answers 400 'out of extra usage', the five-hour session limit is spent, not the model tier: such a probe proves nothing about one entry, which stays in the scope until a later probe answers it. The other entries are OpenRouter models billed to credits. An entry that starts with ~ and ends in -latest is an OpenRouter alias that follows the newest release of one model line. A pinned entry names the newest dated snapshot of its line, because an undated id can resolve to an older snapshot: the `canonical_slug` an id carries in OpenRouter's `/api/v1/models` reply names the snapshot it resolves to. An entry whose id another configured provider also lists carries its provider prefix: pi puts a bare id in the scope once for every provider that lists it, in any letter case, and warns at startup that the pattern `matches several providers`. The saved default stays inside the scope, so new sessions start on it. pi adds an entry to this list when a model outside the scope is saved as the default with Ctrl+S in /model: prune deliberately. A retired alias costs a warning, not an error: `No models match pattern` shows in the startup model scope line and in `/scoped-models`, which resolves this list against the available models. `pi --list-models` does not read this list: it prints every available model, fuzzy-filtered by its optional search argument, so it cannot confirm a scope entry. Every claim about pi in this note holds for pi 1.3.0, checked 2026-10-21.
